You can try K=100, 200 etc.. and evaluate the sensitivity issue.

Other than that I can't think of a reason why results should differ.

regards,
andy

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I am struggling a little bit with year, primary periods, and secondary
periods within pcountOpen in unmarked. All of the examples I've found
are either balanced designs with the same number of secondary periods
(esp J=1), but what about cases when the number of observations per
secondary period varies for each primary period?

For example, I have a dataset with 120 sites each visited on the same
36 occasions over 5 years to count salamanders. However, the time
between observations varied greatly. I can model J = 1 and have 36
primary periods for each site. However, this might not make the most
sense because sometimes observations with only 1 week apart whereas
other times they were months apart. I was thinking about it in terms
of a robust design where the number of observations primary period is
variable. I'm just not sure how to code this in unmarked. Is it
possible to have closed periods within open periods in unmarked?

To be explicit, imagine I had 8 observations where primary periods
have 3, 1, 2, 2 observations within the 4 primary periods. This is
similar than my actual data but has the same idea. Every site has the
same observation schedule. For example, each site might be sampled on
8 occasions where the first three are within one primary period, the
4th occasion is in the 2nd PP, the 5th and 6th observations are in the
3rd PP, and the 7th and 8th observations are in the 4th PP:
1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4

Is it possible to account for this structure? What about the fact that
primary periods are separated by a different number of days?

I don't know if this makes sense, but please let me know if you have
suggestions.
Thanks,
Dan

equally-sized units.

The number of primary periods should not be arbitrary. It should be defined by your understanding of when the population is closed. If the population is not closed at all, then perhaps you should not treat it as such.

For example, if there were 12 observations, and
you specified 4 primary periods, this sets the first 3 observations as
PP 1, observations 4-6 as PP 2, obs 7-9 as PP 3, and obs 10-12 as PP

were equally spaced. Is that correct? The default primary period
matrix would be:

1, 2, 3, 4

Correct

how I could account for that because all sites were sampled on the
same days, at least not with the primaryPeriod option unless I wanted

difference in the amount of time that the population was "open" for?

6, 40, 50, 90,

clarification on any points. I'm not very proficient with R yet, so
making reproducible examples would take me forever.

Dan

Hi Brenda,

I coded up a nonpar bootstrap myself for a model fit with colext(). Here's a sketch of my code in case (BS means bootstrap). I was interested in getting confidence intervals around the occupancy estimates for all years.

Kind regards  --  Marc

BS.sample.size <- 1000        # Bootstrap sample size
results <- array(NA, dim = c(2, 9, BS.sample.size))    # Structure to save results
rownames(results) <- c("finite_sample", "population")
inits <- coef(fm24)        # Use solutions of earlier model fit as inits

for(i in 1:BS.sample.size){        # Do things a large number of times
   cat("\n*** SimRep:", i, "***\n")

   # Generate bootstrap data set with random selection of units
   BS.sel <- sort(sample(1:dim(data.set)[1], size = dim(data.set)[1], replace = TRUE))
   BS.data.set <- data.set[BS.sel,]

   # Generate unmarked data frame
   umfBS <- unmarkedMultFrame(y=BS.data.set[,1:27],
   siteCovs=data.frame(elev = BS.data.set[,"elev"], forest = BS.data.set[,"forest"]),
   yearlySiteCovs=list(year=BS.data.set[,30:38]),
   obsCovs=list(date=BS.data.set[,39:65]),
   numPrimary=9)
   # Using solutions to fm24 for actual data set helps to overcome a local minimum !!!
   # Fit model to boostrap replicate data set
   BSM1 <- colext(~ some model structure , umfBS,
   starts = inits, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=1, maxit = 300), se = FALSE)

   # Save projected and smoothed occupancy estimates
   results[1,,i] <- smoothed(BSM1)[2,]
   results[2,,i] <- projected(BSM1)[2,]
}

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Zero Inflated Poisson in the pcount model
messages.body_plain:
hi Lew,
 (1) Not exactly.   psi is the probability that N is a realization from a Poisson distribution -- so you could still get N=0 in that case.    1-psi is the probability that N is a fixed zero.
 It is true that the marginal expectation of N is lambda*(1-psi).

 (2) I think this is correct -- you would always have the same zero-inflation probability but this leads to different marginal probabilities that N = 0 if you let lambda vary. so there is some flexibility there (i.e., if psi varies by substrate but not lambda, but the model says lambda varies but not psi, then you might get almost equivalent fits)

regards
andy

messages.subject_clean: comment on model selection and another one on local minima
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

first, when using model selection I do this:

models <- fitList(   ... list of some models ... )

ms <- modSel(models)
ms

Now, I have repeatedly found that when executing this for one model set and then for another one (e.g., for some models of detection and then for some with the state parameter(s)), that the object ms was screwed up and did contain models that were not contained in the last call to fitList(). I had to delete the objects model and ms first, and this helped. I can't document this any better, but has any of you made similar observations ?

Second, I've been running a lot of dynamic occupancy models using colext lately. I like the ability to fit such models (much) more quickly than when using BUGS/JAGS and to be able to use AIC for model selection (who knows whether the latter is OK, but everybody is doing it, so ...). However, I have repeatedly found local minima, i.e., the solution provided by unmarked was definitely not the maximum likelihood estimate, even though the convergence code was 0, indicating convergence. How can one know ? Easy sometimes, when the NegLogLike of a more complex model is greater than the NLL of a simpler (typically an adjacent) model. Often, providing initial values has then helped to push the NLL of the more complex model below that of the adjacent model. However, sometimes NOT providing inits got a lower NLL and providing such inits yielded a higher NLL.

So what I am saying is simply this: when fitting complex models, with lots of params (either absolutely, or in relation to the size of the data set), be aware of the dangers of local minima and have an eye on the values of the NLL.

Finally, a question to Richard: colext seems to be using optim internally, because a summary says something about "optim convergence code". However, it does not seem possible to select different optimisation algorithms, e.g., Nelder-Mead, BFGS and so forth. When trying to find global rather than local minima, I thought that playing around with different algorithms could be useful. Do you know whether this is possible in colext ?

Thanks and kind regards  --  Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,

I think you want the independent double observer method, which has the following cell probs:

"10" = p1 * (1-p2)  # detected in first time interval, but not in second
"01" =  (1-p1) * p2 # detected in second time interval, but not in first
"11" = p1 * p2        # detected in both time intervals

Someone please correct me if I'm wrong.

You need to use count data, but it's no problem if it turns out that you don't have any values > 1 in the y matrix. Just make sure that you don't convert integers >1 to 1. Once you estimate lambda, you can obtain an estimate of occurrence probability using the equation:

psi = 1 - exp(-lambda)

Richard

Richard, Andy et al.,

First of all, I have watched the webinar. Thank you very much for
getting that online for those of us who could not attend the live
event. I appreciate the straightforward real life examples that you
provided.

As Richard is aware, I have been using Program Distance for the
analysis of my thesis project studying Northern Goshawks. I am trying
to replicate my work with unmarked for a number of reasons that I
won't go into here.

I may have made some initial design decisions which make the migration
to unmarked less obvious. I am seeking some advice on whether my
survey results can be made to fit the unmarked model.

Background: My objective is to related prey abundance to goshawk
territory occupancy. Based upon a previous study, goshawks within my
study area have a 588ha male home range during the breeding season. I
have therefore placed a 588ha circle centered on the historical nest
tree and am using this as my unit for statistical inference. Within
this circle I randomly placed four 750m line transects which were each
surveyed once over a 9 week period. I originally chose the 4 random
transects to maximize my coverage of the territory and to help ensure
that I was exposed to the various habitat types contained within.

Program Distance allows me to stratify by territory using those four
separate transects, each with separate co-variates, to produce an
estimate for the territory.

I have been able to add the four transects together to generate a
stratified density per territory.

What I have not yet been able to determine:
1. The stratified density estimate (from ranef()) is close to that
produced by Program Distance. However, the confidence intervals do not
represent the uncertainty which occurs as the abundance is scaled up
to the full territory. Are there any plans to enable confidence
interval estimation when the area for inference is larger than the
area covered by the survey?

2. The four surveys were spread over 9 weeks. Via program distance,
the julian date of the survey is an important covariate as was the
observer. Is there any way to put transect specific covariates into a
density estimate for a higher level stratum?

3. Any plans to support observation level covariates?

I assume that both of the first two issues are handled by first
producing transect specific density estimates and then combining the
four estimates and covariates together to produce the estimate for the
stratum with confidence intervals. I have been working to try to
figure out how to do that.

Thank you for any advice you my have.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rob,

(1) If you want to estimate density at a level greater than an individual transect, then you need to include "territory" as a covariate of density and then use predict(), not ranef(). This will give you estimates of density for each territory along with CIs. This will involve estimating many parameters, so you might want to try providing starting values.

(2) You can include both julian date and observer as siteCovs in the analysis. However, I'm not sure how date could affect the distance at which you detect a bird.

(3) What kind of observation-specific covariate could you have? These would need to be specific to each distance band.

One last comment. To properly address all sources of variation in an analysis of the effects of prey density on goshawk occurrence, you would need to jointly analyze the goshawk data and the prey data. The "easiest" way to do this would be to use BUGS or JAGS, but this would be still be pretty hard, and so I think you are on the right track to first try to model goshawk occurrence using *estimates* of prey density.

Best,
Richard

Dear list members,

I sent the following questions to Richard thinking that were not appropriate for the list but Richard suggested me to post it to the list.

Question;

When doing occupancy models and using covariates I have seen people take an average of the occupancy on all the sites to give an unique value of psi.  Is that correct?  How do you get a EE for that approach?  Is it an alternative to take the average of the covariate and plug-in that value in the formula of the best model?

Hi Manuel,

This would be a good question for the list as I'm sure other people have the same question. Anyhow, the approach you mention is fine, but if you only want to make know what proportion of the sites *in the sample* were occupied, it would be better to use the new ranef() function. Something like:

re <- ranef(fm)
mean(bup(re, stat="mode"))
colMeans(confint(re))
